item.passage:
Mrs. Prather repaired chairs in her garage, and on Saturdays she paid Marek four dollars an hour to soak cane, sweep up, and cut out ruined seats. The chair Mr. Nkemelu brought in that week was a plain maple side chair with a hole punched through the middle of its woven seat. "It was my mother's," he said. "Just do it the way it was."

Marek cut the old cane away with a utility knife, working close to the rim so the frame would come clean. As he pulled the stubs out of the holes, he noticed something odd. Most of the strands that ran from front to back went straight across, but near each side two of them stopped short. Instead of reaching the back rail, they ended in holes along the side rails, as if whoever had woven the seat had run out of cane and quit early.

"Somebody cut corners," he said, holding one up.

Mrs. Prather glanced at it from her bench. "Count the holes before you decide that."

He meant to. But the first step of the pattern looked simple: a long strand down through a front hole, across to the back hole facing it, down through that, up through the next one, and back across. He soaked a coil, pegged the end in the hole at the far right, and worked leftward, pleased with how quickly the rows went in. By lunch he could see the trouble. Each new strand leaned a little more than the one before it, and when he reached the last back hole, four front holes were left over with nowhere to go.

He counted then. The front rail had seventeen holes. The back rail had thirteen. The seat was wider at the front than at the back, the way most chair seats are, so that a person sitting has room for both knees.

He sat back on his heels. The short strands had been the answer to that. They filled the extra front holes and ended at the side rails, so that every row could run straight.

It took him the afternoon to pull out his leaning strands and put the rows back in properly, two short ones on each side. When Mr. Nkemelu came for the chair the next Saturday, he ran his hand over the seat and asked whether it had been hard to match.

Marek looked at the short rows near the sides. "Whoever did it the first time knew more than I did," he said, and felt his ears go warm. Mrs. Prather, wiping glue from a chisel, kept her eyes on her work and gave a small nod.

strolls, sure that twenty is a fortune.

though the far curb is only twelve steps off
and they reach it at fifteen, laughing.

and the drivers idle, and she lets them.

At nine a courier on a bicycle
threads the gap between the last two walkers,
and somebody behind him shouts a word
the traffic swallows whole.

At four a man looks up from his phone
and starts out, then thinks better of it,
and rocks on his heels at the curb's edge
like a diver who has changed his mind.

and simply holds up its palm.
The engines rise, the cars roll forward,
and the corner fills again from behind:

with a trumpet, and the number waiting overhead
to be shared out, once more, among
the ones who hurry and the ones who don't.

In the autumn of 1898, Dr. Hannah Merritt, the younger of the two physicians in the mill town of Corvel Falls, asked the town council to make spitting in public an offense punishable by a fine. Her reason was consumption, the disease now called tuberculosis, which had killed eleven people in the town of four thousand that year. Like most doctors of her day, she believed that the disease could spread when spit from a sick person dried on a floor or a sidewalk and rose into the air as dust.

The council was slow to agree. Several members chewed tobacco, as did a good share of the men at the mill, and the general store kept a brass spittoon beside its stove. One councilman asked whether the doctor meant to fine half the voters in town. Another said the rule would be impossible to enforce, since Corvel Falls had one constable and he chewed too.

Dr. Merritt answered with a plan rather than an argument. She asked the council to buy two dozen spittoons, place them in the depot, the post office, the courthouse and the streetcar, and have them emptied and scalded every day. She paid for printed signs herself: SPITTING SPREADS CONSUMPTION. USE THE CUSPIDOR. Only once the spittoons were in place, she proposed, should the fine of one dollar take effect. The council passed the ordinance in January by a vote of five to two.

The record of what followed is thin. The constable's book for 1899 lists four fines for spitting, three of them paid by the same man, and the streetcar company twice reported its spittoons stolen. Yet the habit of spitting on floors, at least in the depot and the post office, seems to have faded within a few years. A visitor in 1904 wrote to her sister that the post office was "clean enough to eat from."

Whether the ordinance saved anyone is harder to say. Deaths from consumption in Corvel Falls fell over the next twenty years, but they fell across most of the country in the same years, in towns with spitting laws and towns without them. Better food, less crowded housing and the care of the sick in sanatoriums all likely played a part. Later research also showed that the disease spreads mainly through the air when a sick person coughs, and much less through dried spit. Dr. Merritt had the route partly wrong.

What she had right was the order of things. She gave the town somewhere to put its habit before she asked it to give the habit up, and she spent her own money on the signs before she spent anyone else's on the fines. A rule people can actually obey, she seems to have understood, is worth more than a stricter one they will simply ignore.
